dl.android.d: The full app, in English and Turkish, following your phone's colours.
dl.android.r2: Testing on Google Play, by invitation while the beta is closed

dl.ios.d: Through the App Store, under the same developer account as macOS.
dl.lede: Free, open source, no account. Pick your device; the one you are using now is marked.
dl.linux.d: Built with Qt 6 for Wayland. It takes its colours, fonts and icons from your desktop: Plasma, Hyprland, Omarchy, GNOME.
dl.linux.r1: A separate package for each family of distributions, 64-bit
dl.macos.d: Apple requires a paid developer account (99 USD a year) to sign and notarise apps. Donations will pay for it.
dl.new.n0: Sending works even when one device's firewall blocks incoming connections: both devices now reach for each other and use the first connection that comes up.
dl.new.n1: A new mark, Dalga: a drop, its waves and the file leaving through a channel. While you send, the file travels the channel.
dl.new.n2: A calmer interface: one highlighted action per screen, no shadows, clearer lists.
dl.new.n3: Fixed the settings screen, which could appear empty.
dl.new.n4: The first Linux app: send and receive with a code or a QR code, following your desktop's theme.
dl.new.nr: Send to anyone, anywhere: devices connect directly across the internet, or through the encrypted relay when a router or firewall is in the way.

dl.verify.title: Check what you install
dl.verify.v1: Get TotalDrop only from Google Play, from this page or from the project's GitHub releases. We do not publish anywhere else.
dl.verify.v2: Every release on GitHub lists SHA-256 checksums. Compare them before you run a file.
dl.verify.v3: Everything is built from the public source code, which you can read and build yourself.
dl.verify.v4: On Linux, install the file you downloaded with sudo pacman -U, sudo apt install ./ or sudo dnf install ./ and its name.
dl.web.d: Receive without installing anything: open a link, type the code, save the files.
dl.windows.d: For Windows 11. The first builds are unsigned, so Windows will warn before the first run until code signing is funded.
don.audit.d1: TotalDrop promises that nobody in between can read your files. A promise like that should be checked by people who did not write the code. Before version 1.0, an independent firm will review the protocol, the cryptography and the code that handles untrusted input, and the full report will be published.
don.audit.d2: Audits of this kind are priced in tens of thousands of dollars; published quotes for similar work go as high as 64,000 USD. We expect 20,000 to 60,000 USD, depending on the firm and the scope. Version 1.0 waits for it.
don.audit.title: The big one: an independent security audit
don.b1.f: The address of the site and of every server, registered at cost with Cloudflare
don.b2.f: The site, the rendezvous server and the relay. Free until relay traffic passes the free daily limits; then 5 USD a month with 1 million requests and 400,000 GB-seconds included
don.b3.f: Apple lets only signed and notarised apps run without warnings on iPhone, iPad and Mac
don.b4.f: Without a signature Windows warns of an unknown publisher. Certum's certificate for open-source developers: 69 EUR the first year with card and reader, 49 EUR after. Microsoft's own service is not offered to individuals outside the US and Canada
don.b5.f: Tells each device its public address, so two devices can connect directly
don.b6.f: The code, automatic builds and release downloads, free for open source
don.b7.f: Publishing the Android app; a one-time fee, already paid
don.budget.title: Every cost, line by line
don.how.h1: Donations go through GitHub Sponsors, once or every month.
don.how.h2: They pay only for the costs on this page. When a cost is added or changes, this page changes first.
don.how.h3: Every month we publish what came in and where it went, here and in the project's repository.
don.how.h4: A donation buys no features, no priority and no influence over the app. Everyone gets the same TotalDrop.
don.how.title: How the money is handled
don.lede: TotalDrop is free for everyone and stays that way: no ads, no premium tier, no investors, no data to sell. Some things still cost money. This page lists every one of them, so you can see exactly what a donation pays for.

hero.lede: TotalDrop moves files directly from your device to theirs, encrypted end to end. You share a short code; nobody in between can read what you send. No account, no email, no phone number.
hero.markTitle: A file leaving the centre through a channel in the waves
hero.title: Send a file straight to another device.
how.note: Across the internet, the two devices connect directly wherever they can. When a router or firewall is in the way, the encrypted transfer goes through our relay, which cannot read it.
how.s1.d: Any type, as many as you like. The receiver gets only what you chose.
how.s2.d: A number and two words, like 7-harbor-rocket. It works once and then expires.
how.s3.d: Both screens show the same four words. If they match, the connection is yours alone.

rm.d1.d: TotalDrop Protocol v0: transfer codes with CPace, Noise XXpsk3 with post-quantum ML-KEM-768, QUIC with single-use keys. Written down so anyone can build a compatible app.
rm.d2.d: Send and receive from a terminal on Linux, macOS and Windows.
rm.d3.d: Send and receive with a code, in English and Turkish, following the phone's colours. On Google Play by invitation.
rm.d4.d: Qt 6 and native Wayland. Follows the theme of KDE Plasma, Hyprland and Omarchy live. Packages for Arch, Debian, Ubuntu and Fedora.
rm.d5.d: Both devices listen and dial, so a firewall on one side no longer stops a transfer.
rm.l1.d: Native apps, once donations cover Apple's developer account.
rm.l2.d: Send to someone who is not online: an encrypted copy waits up to 7 days, and only the link opens it.
rm.l3.d: Optional, Mullvad-style: no email, no phone, no password. Your own devices send to each other without a code.
rm.l3.t: An account that is only a number
rm.l4.d: Pair once, check four words, and send to that person again without a code.
rm.l5.d: Relay only, over Tor, with padded sizes, for people who also need to hide their IP address.
rm.l5.t: Full privacy mode in the apps
rm.lede: Dates are aims, not promises: a feature ships only when it is safe. Every step can be followed in the open repository.
rm.n1.d: Devices find their public address with STUN and connect directly through most home routers. When that is impossible, the encrypted traffic goes through our relay on Cloudflare, which cannot read it.
rm.n2.d: Relay only: the other side never learns your IP address.
rm.n2.t: Privacy mode in the command line
rm.title: What is coming to TotalDrop
rm.v1.d: An outside firm reviews the protocol, the cryptography and the code that handles untrusted input. The full report is published.
rm.v2.d: A ProVerif or Tamarin proof that the hybrid handshake keeps its promises.
rm.v2.t: A formal model of the handshake
rm.v3.d: Device keys add ML-DSA-65 next to Ed25519, so even a future quantum computer cannot impersonate you.
rm.v4.d: People who opt in can use relays run by others, from a signed list.
rm.x1.d: Point the phone at the sender's screen instead of typing the code.
rm.x1.t: Scan the QR code with the camera
rm.x2.d: Open a link, type the code, save the files. Nothing to install, still end-to-end encrypted.
rm.x3.d: A dropped connection picks up where it stopped, without sending what already arrived.
rm.x4.d: A transfer that started through the relay moves to a direct path as soon as one opens.
rm.x5.d: A native Windows 11 app. Signed once donations cover the certificate.
rm.x6.d: Install and update with your AUR helper.

road.p3: iOS and macOS, funded by donations
road.p4: Optional account that is only a random number, for contacts across your devices
road.title: Where we are
sec.f1.d: Files are encrypted on your device and decrypted only on the receiver's. The keys never exist anywhere else.
sec.f2.d: The code turns into a key through a PAKE handshake, so a wrong guess fails at once and the attempt is burned. Key exchange includes post-quantum ML-KEM.
sec.f2.t: The code cannot be guessed offline
sec.f3.d: It sees your IP address and the code's number, never the words, the file names or the files. It keeps no logs.
sec.f4.d: Every line is public. Version 1.0 ships only after an independent security audit.
sec.title: Only you and the receiver can open it
why.cmp.caption: How TotalDrop compares with the usual ways to send a file
why.r1.d: Files go from your device to theirs. No copy waits on a company's server, and no link expires in a week.
why.r2.d: No email, no phone number, no sign-up. A short code is all two devices need.
why.r3.d: Android today, Linux, Windows, macOS and iOS on the way. Phone to laptop, any brand to any brand.
why.r4.d: Whole folders, long videos, original-quality photos. Only your disk and your connection set the limit.
why.r5.d: Four words on both screens prove nobody is in the middle. Encryption is end to end and post-quantum.
why.r6.d: Open source under the GPL, paid for by donations. No ads, no tracking, no premium tier.
why.title: Why TotalDrop
